name: VMT19937 (V-MT19937, X-MT19937, V-SFMT19937)
baseline: std::mt19937_64 (STL-MT19937-64 row) and the reference MT19937 code (ORIG-MT19937 row); Intel MKL generators also shown
workload: Million random samples per second for 32-bit MT19937, 64-bit MT19937-64 and SFMT19937 families, in a scalar one-value-per-call mode and a 'vectorial' bulk-fill mode, on SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512, NEON and SVE256.
claimed_speedup: 64-bit, bulk-fill mode: STL-MT19937-64 317 M/s (AVX2) vs V-MT19937-64 1161 M/s and X-MT19937-64 827 M/s; AVX-512 590 vs 2865 M/s (about 3.7x and 4.9x, derived from page data). 64-bit scalar mode AVX2: 317 vs 372 M/s (1.17x, derived). 32-bit bulk fill AVX2: ORIG-MT19937 259 M/s vs V-MT19937 2392 M/s (9.2x, derived); V-SFMT19937 reaches 10943 M/s on AVX-512 vs ORIG-MT19937 418 M/s.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the tables (README only says the build needs GCC 13+, Clang 16+ or MSVC 2022 with /std:c++20).
hardware: x86-64 with SSE4.2 / AVX2 / AVX-512 and ARM64 NEON / SVE256; CPU models not stated in the README.
tradeoffs: C++20 header-only. The V family changes the output stream: it polls several de-phased MT19937 instances (jump-ahead by polynomial, about 4 KB of jump data per width) in round-robin, so it is not bit-identical to MT19937. The X family vectorizes one MT state and keeps the exact MT19937 / MT19937-64 / SFMT19937 sequence. Fixing VRegBitLen gives the same stream on any ISA. Needs SIMD for the big wins; Intel MKL is faster at 32-bit AVX-512 bulk (6479 vs 5742 M/s for V-MT19937).
caveats: Tier C because the README does not name the CPUs, compiler or flags behind the tables (the accompanying arXiv paper 2309.16682 may; arxiv.org was blocked in this run). Most large speedups are bulk-fill mode; scalar-mode gains are 1.2x to 2x. 32-bit rows compare to the reference MT19937 C code rather than std::mt19937. The repo bundles reference MT19937 and SFMT 1.5.1 sources for the comparison.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'PRNG benchmark comparison mt19937 xoshiro PCG wyrand results' surfaced the paper 'VMT19937: A SIMD-Friendly Pseudo Random Number Generator based on Mersenne Twister 19937'; repo README and commit page then opened.

name: SFMT (SIMD-oriented Fast Mersenne Twister)
baseline: MT19937-64 reference code (same generator as std::mt19937_64) and 32-bit MT19937
workload: CPU time to generate 1e9 64-bit unsigned integers with SFMT19937-64 (SIMD) vs MT19937-64, from the MELG-64 authors' comparison; plus 32-bit bulk-fill throughput of ORIG-SFMT19937 vs ORIG-MT19937 in the VMT19937 README.
claimed_speedup: MELG-64 README table: SFMT19937-64 with SIMD 1.8457 s vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s on Intel Core i7-3770 (2.8x, derived from page data) and 2.8806 s vs 6.6490 s on AMD Phenom II X6 1045T (2.3x, derived). VMT19937 README: ORIG-SFMT19937 bulk 1444 M/s vs ORIG-MT19937 161 M/s on SSE4.2 and 4445 vs 418 M/s on AVX-512 (about 9x to 11x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 on Linux (MELG-64 README table); compiler version not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 3.40GHz and AMD Phenom II X6 1045T 2.70GHz (MELG-64 README).
stars_or_usage: 96 stars; widely ported (Erlang, Rust, Objective-C and others)
tradeoffs: Different output sequence than MT19937 (128-bit-oriented recurrence); fill-array API wants 16-byte aligned arrays; SSE2, AVX 256, NEON and Altivec backends (README says big-endian and Altivec are untested); many Mersenne exponents (607 to 216091); jump-ahead code in jump/. The MELG-64 README notes SFMT has a large high-dimensional equidistribution gap for 64-bit output.
caveats: The SFMT repo itself contains no benchmark numbers; the figures are third-party (the MELG-64 table is by Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 2018; the VMT19937 table does not name its CPU). The authors' own MCQMC 2006 paper was not opened in this run. 'abandoned' is by commit date (last 2021); the code is stable and widely used.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'SFMT SIMD-oriented Fast Mersenne Twister github benchmark faster than MT19937'; timings harvested from the sharase/melg-64 and fabiocannizzo/VMT19937 READMEs.

name: MELG-64 (MELG19937-64)
baseline: MT19937-64 reference code (same generator as std::mt19937_64)
workload: CPU time in seconds to generate 1e9 64-bit unsigned integers.
claimed_speedup: MELG19937-64 4.2123 s vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s on Intel Core i7-3770 (1.2x, derived from page data); 6.2920 s vs 6.6490 s on AMD Phenom II X6 1045T (1.06x, derived). README: 'Fast generation competitive with MT19937-64'. SFMT19937-64 with SIMD is faster still (1.8457 s and 2.8806 s).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 on Linux; compiler version not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 3.40GHz; AMD Phenom II X6 1045T 2.70GHz.
tradeoffs: Scalar C, 312-word state like MT19937-64, jump-ahead (default skip 2^256), variants from 2^607-1 to 2^19937-1 periods. The point of the design is maximal equidistribution (Delta = 0 vs 7820 for MT19937-64), with speed only modestly better than MT19937-64.
caveats: Speed gain over MT19937-64 is small (6% to 21%). Measurements are on old CPUs (2012-era Intel, 2010-era AMD) and do not include xoshiro or PCG. The README cites the peer-reviewed article (Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 2018); the article itself was not opened in this run. Last commit 2023, stable research code.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page github.com/topics/prng (C) listed sharase/melg-64; README opened.

name: FastShuffleExperiments (nearly divisionless bounded random integers and shuffle)
baseline: std::shuffle (libstdc++ as of the paper, divide-based uniform_int_distribution) and OpenBSD-style / Java-style bounded-random algorithms
workload: Shuffling arrays of 32-bit and 64-bit elements, sizes 5 to 1e9, nanoseconds per array element, every variant, including std::shuffle through a UniformRandomBitGenerator wrapper, draws from the same lehmer64 generator (cpp/shuffle.cpp).
claimed_speedup: Sample results.txt in TOMACS_RCR/README.md, array size 10000, 32-bit indexes: nearly divisionless 1.80 ns/element vs OpenBSD-like 5.32, Java-like 2.98, std::shuffle 18.57 (std::shuffle about 10x slower, derived from page data); 64-bit indexes: 1.78 vs 14.40, 7.97 and 15.23 (std::shuffle about 8.6x slower, derived). README notes the exact numbers will vary.
compiler_and_flags: g++ or clang++ with -std=c++11 -O3 (cpp/Makefile); compiler version not stated.
hardware: Not stated (README shows sample output only; advises Linux, TurboBoost and hyperthreading off).
stars_or_usage: 41 stars; algorithm adopted by libstdc++, Abseil, Swift, Go, Julia, Zig and NumPy per the README
tradeoffs: Benchmark and experiment code for Lemire's multiply-and-reject method (needs 128-bit multiply; 'nearly divisionless'), not a packaged library. The idea is easy to copy into any PRNG wrapper.
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (ACM TOMACS 2019, 'Fast Random Integer Generation in an Interval') with a replication package, but the numbers on the page are an illustrative sample run and the CPU is not stated. The std::shuffle baseline reflects libstdc++ before it adopted this very technique, so the gap against a current libstdc++ is smaller. The benchmark generator is lehmer64, not std::mt19937, so the std::shuffle column isolates the range-reduction cost.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page github.com/topics/shuffle (C++) listed lemire/FastShuffleExperiments; WebSearch 'github faster than std::uniform_int_distribution bounded random C++ benchmark library' surfaced lemire/simple_cpp_shuffle_benchmark, whose README links the same paper.

name: cpp_prngs (RomuDuoJr, QuarkBurst64, Konadare192, PCG32, xoshiro256** engines with a Random<E> front end)
baseline: std::mt19937 (also std::mt19937_64, std::minstd_rand, std::default_random_engine, C rand(), std::uniform_int_distribution)
workload: Quick Bench micro-benchmarks reported as CPU time / no-op time: raw engine next(), bounded integers in [0, bound), and bounded floats.
claimed_speedup: Values read by eye from the README bar charts (approximate): raw next() std::mt19937 about 13,000 vs RomuDuoJr about 2,700, QuarkBurst64 about 2,600, xoshiro256** about 4,200, PCG32 about 5,000 (lower is faster; roughly 5x for RomuDuoJr, derived from the chart). Bounded integers: UniformIntDistribution<std::mt19937> about 17,000 vs RandomBounded<RomuDuoJr> about 3,400 (roughly 5x, derived). README text: 'All of the included engines substantially outperform the standard-library generators'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (Quick Bench; benchmark sources in benchmarks/).
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17, constexpr-capable, 4 to 32 bytes of state, Lemire bounded integers, Arduino AVR support. The engines are ports of other authors' designs (RomuDuoJr by M. Overton, Konadare192px++ by P. Evensen, QuarkBurst by W. S. Parsons, SmallFast by B. Jenkins); Romu, Konadare and QuarkBurst are less scrutinized than xoshiro or PCG.
caveats: Numbers exist only as bar charts from Quick Bench with no hardware, compiler or flags; I read the PNGs by eye. The fastest engines are ports, so the entry mainly curates third-party winners. The upstream eightomic/quarkburst GitHub page returned 404 when opened in this run. The README cites a 47-PRNG 'RNG Battle Royale (2020)' shootout by Rhet Butler that ranks RomuDuoJr first; that page could not be opened here. Third-party engine headers keep their own licenses (public domain, Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause per README).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'github romu random C header RomuTrio RomuDuoJr implementation benchmark'.

name: seiran128 (Seiran PRNG)
baseline: xoshiro256**, PCG64 (pcg64_xsh_rr) and MT19937-64 reference code
workload: Speed of 64-bit outputs per nanosecond measured with the xoshiro/xoroshiro harness.c, ten generators compared in one table.
claimed_speedup: seiran128 1.20 64-bit/ns vs xoshiro256** 0.99, pcg64_xsh_rr 0.38, mt19937_64 0.32 (about 1.2x xoshiro256** and 3.2x PCG64, derived from page data). README: 'About 3.7 times faster than Mersenne Twister (64-bit version)'. Not faster than sfc64 (1.21) in the same table.
tradeoffs: 16 bytes of state, period 2^128-1, LFSR-style with no 128-bit multiply; jump function for 2^64 steps; 64-bit only (no 32-bit variant); not cryptographic (state recovered from 3 outputs with Z3 per the README). Public domain, no patent grant.
caveats: First-party numbers; the xoshiro harness link was not opened and flags are unstated; one 2018-era laptop CPU. Author says the design has not been investigated by others. Five commits, last in 2021. Quality claims (PractRand 32 TB, BigCrush) are the author's own.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page github.com/topics/prng (C) listed andanteyk/prng-seiran; README and commit history opened.

name: shioi128 (Shioi PRNG)
baseline: xoshiro256**, PCG64 (pcg64_xsh_rr) and MT19937-64 reference code
workload: Speed of 64-bit outputs per nanosecond measured with the xoshiro/xoroshiro harness.c, same ten-generator table as seiran.
claimed_speedup: shioi128 1.00 64-bit/ns vs xoshiro256** 0.99, pcg64_xsh_rr 0.38, mt19937_64 0.32 (about parity with xoshiro256**, 2.6x PCG64, derived from page data). README: 'About 3.1 times faster than Mersenne Twister (64 bit version)'.
tradeoffs: 16 bytes of state, period 2^128-1; needs a 64-bit constant multiply (slow on some targets); constant-time jump of 2^64 steps costs about one next(); 32-bit variants incomplete; not cryptographic (Z3 attack failed in a day per README).
caveats: Roughly equal to xoshiro256** in speed, so it only beats PCG64 and the Mersenne Twisters; first-party numbers, flags unstated, one laptop CPU. Four commits, last in 2019. Sibling of seiran128 (same author, same table).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): Linked from the seiran README comparison table; repo README and commit history opened.

name: dqrng (xoshiro256++ / PCG64 generators and fast distributions; C++ header-only, R package)
baseline: R's built-in RNG (Mersenne Twister with R's rnorm and sample.int)
workload: bench::mark from R: rnorm(1e4) vs dqrnorm(1e4); sample.int(1e7, 1e5) and sample.int(1e10, 1e5) with and without replacement vs dqsample.int.
claimed_speedup: rnorm(1e4) median 654.7 us vs dqrnorm 85.9 us (7.6x, derived from page data); sample.int(1e7, 1e5, replace=TRUE) 7.07 ms vs dqsample.int 296.86 us (24x, derived); sample.int(1e7, 1e5) without replacement 42.8 ms vs dqsample.int 679.1 us (63x, derived).
tradeoffs: The RNG and distribution code is a C++ header-only library usable from C++ (xoshiro.h is CC0, pcg_* headers are Apache-2.0 or MIT per LICENSE.note), but the package as a whole is AGPL-3.0 strong copyleft. R-centric API (registers as a user-supplied R RNG).
caveats: Baseline is R's generators, not std::mt19937 or xoshiro/PCG. No hardware or compiler stated. The speedups combine different engines and different distribution algorithms, not just the generator. Timings are median R microbenchmarks from the README.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic pages github.com/topics/rng (C++) and github.com/topics/random (C++) listed daqana/dqrng; README opened.

name: simdrng (XoshiroSIMD, Philox and ChaCha SIMD generators)
baseline: scalar xoshiro256++ and std::mt19937_64 (also std::uniform_real_distribution for doubles)
workload: Google Benchmark results on a CI runner: u64 buffer fill (4096 values per call, derived from items/s x time), per-call latency, and double generation, scalar vs SIMD vs MT19937_64.
claimed_speedup: GCC 15 JSON on AMD EPYC 7763: XoshiroSIMD fill_u64 1645 ns (2.49 G values/s) vs scalar xoshiro fill_u64 3835 ns (1.07 G values/s), 2.3x (derived from page data); per-call std MT19937_64 1.598 ns vs scalar xoshiro 0.936 ns; xoshiro uniform() double 1.32 ns vs 4.65 ns through the std double path vs MT19937_64 std double 8.01 ns (3.5x and 6.1x, derived). The SIMD per-call u64 path (2.81 ns) is slower than scalar.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 15 (also gcc-14, clang-19, clang-20 result folders); CMake 'bench' preset: Release with -march=x86-64-v3; benchmark JSON says library_build_type release.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor, 4-vCPU GitHub-hosted runner at 2445 MHz (cpu_model.txt in the results folder).
tradeoffs: C++20 header-only with xsimd runtime dispatch (AVX-512, AVX2, NEON) and nanobind Python bindings that act as numpy.random.Generator; SIMD only pays off for bulk fills (per-call SIMD is about 3x slower than scalar). Four families: Xoshiro256++, SplitMix64, ChaCha, Philox. Pre-1.0 API.
caveats: Numbers come from one CI run (20260722T164804Z) on a shared virtual machine, so noise is likely. Ratios are my derivations from the JSON. The MT19937_64 comparison is per-call, the SIMD win is in bulk fill. Benchmark names for the std double path were interpreted from the README text. libstdc++ is inferred from GCC on Linux.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page github.com/topics/philox listed DiamonDinoia/simdrng; benchmark-results branch JSON and CMake presets opened.

name: vphilox (SIMD Philox4x32-10 counter-based engine)
baseline: std::mt19937 (PCG64 and xoshiro256++ in the same table)
workload: Cost per byte (RDTSC reference cycles) of bulk generate_n and per-value operator() relative to std::mt19937 on the same machine, five CPUs.
claimed_speedup: Cost relative to std::mt19937 (lower is faster), generate_n: 0.75x Raspberry Pi 5 NEON, 0.38x Sapphire Rapids, 0.22x Skylake-SP, 0.24x Cascade Lake 4 vCPU, 0.33x Cascade Lake 32 vCPU. Same machines, PCG64: 0.83x, 0.59x, 0.33x, 0.32x, 0.53x; xoshiro256++: 0.28x, 0.30x, 0.24x, 0.17x, 0.29x. README: buffer fill runs at 1.3x to 4.6x the throughput of std::mt19937; vphilox beats xoshiro256++ only on Skylake-SP (0.4210 vs 0.4703 cycles/byte).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (Ubuntu 24.04) in the Skylake-SP and Sapphire Rapids environment files; CMake 'bench' preset (Release, full optimization), exact flags not opened. Raw JSON and environment files are in results/.
hardware: Raspberry Pi 5 (NEON); Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C (Sapphire Rapids); Intel Xeon 2.00GHz family 6 model 85 stepping 3 (Skylake-SP, 4 vCPU GCP); Cascade Lake (family 6 model 85 stepping 7) on a 4-vCPU slice and a 32-vCPU two-socket host.
tradeoffs: C++20 header-only. Counter-based Philox with bit-exact output across compilers, OSes, CPUs and thread counts, O(1) discard/seek, text checkpoint save/restore, per-thread streams without locks. AVX-512, AVX2, NEON and scalar backends. Use generate_n for the speed; per-value operator() costs 0.51x to 1.15x of std::mt19937. Slower than xoshiro256++ on four of five CPUs.
caveats: Very new, one author, not yet tagged, no stars. All numbers are first-party. Cycles per byte uses RDTSC reference cycles and is only comparable inside one machine. Per-value drawing on Pi 5 is 0.87x the speed of std::mt19937. Compiler details were only checked on two x86 environment files. libstdc++ inferred from GCC on Linux.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page github.com/topics/philox listed sinhaparth5/vphilox; README, docs/benchmarks/README.md, environment files and CMake presets opened.

name: EigenRand (vectorized random distributions and engines for Eigen)
baseline: std::mt19937_64 with the equivalent C++ std distributions (std::normal_distribution, std::uniform_int_distribution, std::generate_canonical and so on); Eigen's Random for 'balanced'
workload: Filling Eigen matrices with random values from about 30 univariate distributions; charts show speed-up of EigenRand over the std (or Eigen) reference on three platforms.
claimed_speedup: README: '5~10 times faster than non-vectorized functions'. Ubuntu GCC chart, values read by eye (approximate): uniformReal about 22x, normal(0,1) about 8x, uniformInt(0~63) about 10x, cauchy about 15x, binomial(20,0.5) about 24x, discrete(fp32) about 32x; several only about 1.6x to 1.7x (chiSquared, gamma(10.5,1), fisherF(5,5), uniformInt(0~100k)).
compiler_and_flags: Ubuntu 18.04 GCC 7.5.0 with AVX2; Windows 2019 MSVC 19.29.30147 with AVX2; macOS Monterey clang 13.1.6 with NEON; Eigen 3.4.0. CMake Release uses -O3 -DNDEBUG for GCC/Clang; target flags (e.g. -mavx2) via EIGENRAND_CXX_FLAGS, exact value for the charts not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C (Ubuntu), Intel Xeon Platinum 8171M (Windows), Apple M1 Pro (macOS).
tradeoffs: Header-only, needs Eigen 3.3.4 to 5.0.x; SSE, AVX2, AVX-512 and NEON. Uses its own vectorized algorithms, so sequences differ from std distributions, and vectorized math has small precision loss (README measures Earth Mover's distance in an Accuracy section). Also ships vectorized Mersenne Twister engines Vmt19937_64 and P8_mt19937_64.
caveats: Only the Ubuntu/GCC chart was inspected; bar heights are read by eye (the exact values are on a GitHub Actions page that was not opened). The libc++ and MSVC STL entries rely on the README's platform list and were not checked chart by chart. Speedups range from 1.6x to 32x depending on distribution. The benchmark (benchmark/benchmark.cpp) uses std::mt19937_64 as the std engine.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page github.com/topics/random-number-generators listed bab2min/EigenRand ('Fastest Random Distribution Generator for Eigen'); README, CMakeLists.txt, benchmark.cpp and the Ubuntu chart opened.

name: ra_prng / ra_core (array-based addressable PRNG)
workload: bench_release.c on one pinned core: seed-plus-generate cost for batches of K=1 and K=255 words per key (reinit on every call) and for long streams, ns per word.
claimed_speedup: ra_core_singleblock K=255: 0.191 ns/word (20018 MB/s) vs xoshiro256** 1.30 ns/word (2937 MB/s) and Philox4x32-10 3.79 ns/word; README states about 6.8x faster than xoshiro256** and 19.9x faster than Philox in that regime. K=1: 1.13x faster than Philox but 1.77x slower than xoshiro256**. ra_core_orbit long stream: 3.87 ns/word vs xoshiro256** 1.20 ns/word (about 3.2x slower).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2.0, -O3 -march=native, pinned with taskset -c 0, min of 5 to 7 trials plus best of 8 outer runs (benchmark file experiments/2026-9-1_family-productionization/bench_release.c).
tradeoffs: About 2 KB state (two 256-entry arrays that permute each other); random-access addressable initialization (key + addr_hi); wins only for many short batches that reseed, loses to xoshiro256** for continuous streams; no SIMD or GPU version; not cryptographic; Python bindings compile with -march=native at install.
caveats: Very new repo (first commit 2026-08-25); the commit history lists an AI assistant as co-author. The README admits an earlier 30303 MB/s claim was not reproducible and that a benchmark fairness bug (inlining of reference baselines) was found and fixed on 2026-09-12. Self-reported only; the 'accepted but unpublished' paper could not be checked. CC BY-NC-SA is non-OSI and non-commercial, so the code must not be copied.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page github.com/topics/prng (C) listed ooalahhq/ra_prng; README and commit history opened.

name: xoshiro256++ via david-cortes/xoshiro_cpp, as measured in zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks
baseline: std::mt19937_64 (also std::mt19937, std::minstd_rand, std::ranlux48, C rand())
workload: Mean time per generated 64-bit value, Google Benchmark, 100 repetitions, code written to prevent compiler tricks; about 20 generators compared.
claimed_speedup: xoshiro256++ 1.06 ns +/- 0.002 (946.7M/s) vs std::mt19937_64 3.40 ns +/- 0.028 (294.3M/s) and std::mt19937 3.70 ns (about 3.2x, derived from page data); README labels it 'Fastest for 64 bits, good quality'.
tradeoffs: The wrapper makes xoshiro256++ and xoshiro128++ usable with <random> distributions, jump and state serialization; the repo's seeding differs slightly from Vigna's original.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project (prng.di.unimi.it is on the known list); reported as is_evidence_for_known. The benchmark repo (zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks) is AGPL-3.0, last commit 2023-06-08, no SIMD flags, standard library unstated, old 2012 CPU. The wrapper repo's own last commit date and stars were not re-checked for this entry (1 star seen).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'github PRNG shootout benchmark C++ xoshiro256 PCG64 sfc64 romu wyrand speed table' surfaced zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks; README.adoc opened and its table quoted.

name: PCG (pcg_cpp::pcg32_fast and others) as measured in zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks
baseline: std::mt19937 and std::mt19937_64 (also std::minstd_rand, std::ranlux48, C rand())
workload: Mean time per generated value, Google Benchmark, 100 repetitions, about 20 generators compared.
claimed_speedup: pcg_cpp::pcg32_fast 0.933 ns +/- 0.006 (1071.97M/s) vs std::mt19937 3.70 ns +/- 0.048 (270.65M/s), about 4.0x (derived from page data); pcg32 1.09 ns; pcg64_fast 1.31 ns and pcg64 1.98 ns vs std::mt19937_64 3.40 ns (2.6x and 1.7x, derived). README: 'PCG is superior in all aspects for non-cryptographic uses'.
tradeoffs: PCG variants differ in state size and speed (pcg32_fast is the fastest 32-bit variant here, pcg64 the slowest 64-bit one in this table); the same table also lists wjakob pcg32 (1.06 ns) and pcg32_8 (8.48 ns, AVX path not usable on this CPU).
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project (imneme/pcg-cpp is on the known list); reported as is_evidence_for_known. Same single-CPU, standard-library-unstated benchmark as the xoshiro entry; zeFresk benchmark repo is AGPL-3.0 and has not been updated since 2023-06-08. Last commit date of pcg-cpp not re-checked for this entry.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'github PRNG shootout benchmark C++ xoshiro256 PCG64 sfc64 romu wyrand speed table' surfaced zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks; README.adoc opened and its table quoted.
